BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- The United Nations Sunday launched a special tribunal to prosecute the assassins of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri. A statue of slain former Lebanese prime minister Rafiq Hariri stands in Beirut. The tribunal convened at The Hague more than four years after Hariri was killed in a massive car bombing in Beirut on February 14, 2005. The bomb, detonated as Hariri's armored motorcade passed through Beirut's fashionable seaside Corniche district, contained hundreds of pounds of explosives. It left buildings shattered and streets littered with the mangled wreckage of vehicles. The blast also killed 22 other people. The Lebanese army was out in force on the streets of Beirut Sunday as people turned out to pay their respects to Hariri, who is buried downtown in the Lebanese capital. The U.N. tribunal will have 11 judges, whose identities are being kept secret for their safety. Four will be Lebanese. The prosecution could take as long as 10 years, sources close to the tribunal said. Four senior Lebanese generals are being held over the bombing, which also killed 22 other people. But many Lebanese -- as well as the United States and U.N. investigators -- believe Syria ordered the assassination. Syria denies it. The tribunal's prosecutor, Daniel Bellemare, refused to commit when asked at a news conference Sunday if Syrians would be charged. He said the public would have to wait and see. The U.S. State Department pledged its continued support of Lebanese judicial authorities and the tribunal's operations. The United States has promised to contribute $14 million; a request for an additional $6 million is pending approval from Congress. In a statement issued Sunday, acting State Department spokesman Robert A. Wood said Hariri's death "was an unsuccessful attempt to undermine Lebanon's sovereignty." He added: "The Lebanese people answered his assassination with the Cedar Revolution, leading to the withdrawal of Syrian troops and the most democratic Lebanese elections in decades." At the time of Hariri's death, neighboring Syria had immense political influence in the country, and had maintained troops in its smaller neighbor since the 1980s, after the fighting between Israel and the PLO in Lebanon. Hariri was admired for spearheading the rebuilding of Beirut after the country's civil war, from 1975 to 1990, and many Lebanese blamed Syria for the killing, citing Hariri's patriotism and strong sense of Lebanese independence. The killing sparked widespread protests that led to the eventual withdrawal of Syrian troops from Lebanon and the election of an anti-Syrian bloc in parliament. The anti-Syrian movement is known as the March 14 Alliance, named after the day millions of supporters of Hariri took to the streets, and its actions have been dubbed the Cedar Revolution, for the nation's iconic cedar trees. Huge counter-protests also were staged by Lebanese supporters of Syria. Along the way, U.N. investigators tasked to probe the attack found links between Syria's government and Hariri's assassination. The Lebanese hope the tribunal will settle the case, but there are also fears it could further divide the nation and open up older wounds in the country. The special tribunal takes over from the Beirut-based International Independent Investigation Commission, which looked into 20 other attacks and found elements linking some of them to a criminal network behind the Hariri killing, the United Nations said. The trial will take place in a converted gymnasium in a suburb of The Hague. The U.N. says the case is expected to be ready for trial by 2010. --CNN's Cal Perry contributed to this report.

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) — On Sunday, the United Nations inaugurated a special court tasked with trying those responsible for the assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri.

In Beirut, a statue commemorates the slain former leader, also spelled Rafiq Hariri. The tribunal opened in The Hague more than four years after Hariri was killed on February 14, 2005, in a huge car bomb attack in Beirut. The explosives, weighing hundreds of pounds, were set off as Hariri’s armored convoy moved through the city’s upscale seaside Corniche area. The explosion smashed nearby buildings and left the streets strewn with twisted vehicle debris. Twenty-two other people also died in the attack.

On Sunday, Lebanese army forces were heavily deployed across Beirut as crowds gathered to honor Hariri, who is buried in the downtown area of the Lebanese capital.

The U.N.-backed court will be made up of 11 judges, four of whom will be Lebanese. Their names are being withheld for security reasons. Sources close to the tribunal said the prosecution process could last up to a decade.

Four senior Lebanese generals are being detained in connection with the bombing, which killed Hariri and 22 others. However, many people in Lebanon, along with the United States and U.N. investigators, believe Syria directed the assassination. Syria has rejected the accusation.

Daniel Bellemare, the tribunal’s prosecutor, declined at a Sunday news conference to say whether Syrians would face charges, telling the public it would have to wait for developments.

The U.S. State Department said it would continue backing both Lebanese judicial officials and the work of the tribunal. Washington has pledged $14 million, and Congress is considering a request for another $6 million.

In a statement released Sunday, acting State Department spokesman Robert A. Wood described Hariri’s killing as “an unsuccessful attempt to undermine Lebanon’s sovereignty.” He said the Lebanese public responded to the assassination through the Cedar Revolution, which helped bring about the departure of Syrian forces and produced Lebanon’s most democratic elections in decades.

When Hariri was killed, Syria, Lebanon’s neighbor, held major political sway in the country and had kept troops there since the 1980s, following fighting in Lebanon between Israel and the PLO. Hariri was widely respected for leading efforts to reconstruct Beirut after Lebanon’s 1975-1990 civil war. Many Lebanese accused Syria of involvement in his death, pointing to Hariri’s strong patriotism and commitment to Lebanese independence.

The assassination triggered mass demonstrations that eventually resulted in the withdrawal of Syrian troops from Lebanon and the election of an anti-Syrian parliamentary bloc. That movement became known as the March 14 Alliance, named for the date when millions of Hariri supporters filled the streets. Its campaign was called the Cedar Revolution, a reference to Lebanon’s symbolic cedar trees. Lebanese supporters of Syria also organized large counter-demonstrations.

During the investigation, U.N. investigators assigned to examine the bombing identified connections between the Syrian government and Hariri’s murder. Many Lebanese hope the tribunal will bring the case to a conclusion, though some worry it may deepen divisions within the country and reopen old conflicts.

The special tribunal replaces the International Independent Investigation Commission based in Beirut. According to the United Nations, that commission investigated 20 other attacks and found signs that some were connected to a criminal network involved in Hariri’s killing.

The proceedings will be held in a converted gymnasium in a suburb of The Hague. The U.N. has said the case is expected to be ready for trial by 2010.

CNN’s Cal Perry contributed to this report.

**UN-backed tribunal opens in The Hague to prosecute Hariri assassination suspects**

**THE HAGUE, Netherlands** — A United Nations-backed tribunal formally opened in The Hague on Sunday to prosecute those accused of carrying out the 2005 assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, a killing that plunged Lebanon into political crisis and reshaped the country’s relations with Syria.

The Special Tribunal for Lebanon is the first international court established to try a political assassination as a terrorist crime. It will investigate and prosecute those responsible for the February 14, 2005, bombing on Beirut’s seafront that killed Hariri and 21 others, and wounded more than 200 people.

Hariri, a billionaire businessman and dominant figure in Lebanese politics, was killed when a massive explosion struck his motorcade near the St. George Hotel. The attack sparked widespread protests in Lebanon, known as the Cedar Revolution, and led to the withdrawal of Syrian troops after nearly three decades in the country.

UN officials have described the tribunal as a milestone in the fight against impunity, saying it offers a legal path to accountability after years of political tension and competing accusations surrounding the case.

The court, based outside Lebanon for security and political reasons, will apply Lebanese criminal law while operating with international judges and prosecutors. It was created through an agreement between the United Nations and Lebanon and later brought into force by the UN Security Council.

The tribunal’s launch comes after years of investigation by UN-appointed teams. No defendants were immediately in custody at the court’s opening, and officials said proceedings could take time as prosecutors review evidence and prepare indictments.

Hariri’s killing has remained one of the most consequential events in Lebanon’s modern history. Supporters of the tribunal say it is essential to uncovering the truth and deterring future political violence. Critics, including some factions in Lebanon, have questioned whether the court could deepen divisions in an already fragile political system.

For Hariri’s family and supporters, the opening of the tribunal marks a long-awaited step toward justice.

“This is not only about one man,” a UN official said in remarks marking the court’s launch. “It is about the principle that political murder cannot be met with silence.”

**BEIRUT —** A United Nations-backed tribunal opened its work Sunday to prosecute those responsible for the 2005 assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, a killing that transformed Lebanon’s political landscape, forced Syria to end nearly three decades of military presence in the country and drew sustained backing from the United States and its allies.

The Special Tribunal for Lebanon, based in The Hague, formally began operating after years of political deadlock, security fears and diplomatic wrangling over how to try suspects in one of the Middle East’s most consequential political killings.

Hariri, a billionaire businessman and dominant figure in post-civil-war Lebanon, was killed on Feb. 14, 2005, when a massive truck bomb struck his motorcade along Beirut’s seafront. The explosion killed him and 21 others, wounded more than 200 people and devastated a stretch of the capital that Hariri had helped rebuild after Lebanon’s 1975-1990 civil war.

His assassination immediately shook Lebanon and the wider region. Many Lebanese opponents of Syrian influence blamed Damascus, which had maintained troops and intelligence networks in Lebanon since the civil war era. Syria denied involvement, but international pressure mounted quickly.

In the weeks after the bombing, hundreds of thousands of Lebanese took to the streets in demonstrations that became known as the **Cedar Revolution**. Protesters demanded the truth about Hariri’s killing, the withdrawal of Syrian forces and an end to Syrian dominance over Lebanese political life. The rallies culminated in one of the largest public gatherings in Lebanon’s history, centered in Beirut’s Martyrs’ Square.

Under intense domestic and international pressure, Syria withdrew its troops from Lebanon in April 2005, ending a military presence that had lasted nearly 29 years. The withdrawal was widely viewed as a major geopolitical shift, though Syrian influence in Lebanon remained a deeply divisive issue through political allies and regional power networks.

The tribunal’s creation was backed strongly by the United States, France and other Western governments, which argued that an international court was necessary because Lebanon’s judiciary could not safely or independently handle such a politically explosive case. Washington repeatedly described the court as a tool to end impunity for political assassinations in Lebanon and to support Lebanese sovereignty.

U.S. officials have also framed the tribunal as part of broader support for Lebanon’s elected institutions, particularly after the country’s pro-Western and anti-Syrian political bloc, known as the March 14 movement, emerged from the Cedar Revolution. That coalition, named for the date of the huge 2005 rally, made the Hariri investigation a central demand.

The tribunal is unusual in international law because it focuses on a single attack and applies Lebanese criminal law, while operating under U.N. authority. It was established after Lebanon’s political factions failed to ratify the agreement domestically, leading the U.N. Security Council to bring it into force.

The start of the court’s work is expected to revive political tensions in Lebanon, where Hariri’s killing remains a national trauma and where rival camps disagree sharply over the tribunal’s legitimacy and purpose. Supporters say it offers the best hope of accountability after a series of assassinations targeting anti-Syrian politicians, journalists and security officials. Critics, including Syria’s allies in Lebanon, have accused the court of being politicized and serving Western interests.

No convictions have yet been secured at the opening of proceedings, and investigators have faced a complex trail involving intelligence claims, telecommunications evidence and shifting political pressures. Earlier U.N. inquiries suggested the assassination required a high level of organization, but determining who ordered and executed the attack has remained the central challenge.

For many Lebanese, the tribunal’s launch is about more than one killing. Hariri’s assassination marked the beginning of a turbulent era that included Syria’s withdrawal, political polarization, war between Israel and Hezbollah in 2006, repeated government crises and continuing disputes over Lebanon’s sovereignty and alignment in the region.

In Beirut, the opening of the tribunal is likely to be watched with a mixture of hope, suspicion and anxiety. For Hariri’s supporters, it represents a long-awaited step toward justice. For others, it raises fears that the pursuit of accountability could deepen Lebanon’s sectarian and political divisions.

Nearly four years after the blast that killed Hariri, the court’s first task is to prove that an international tribunal can deliver credible justice in a case that has already reshaped Lebanon’s history.

**HARIRI TRIBUNAL OPENS IN THE HAGUE AMID LEBANON TENSIONS**

**LEIDSCHENDAM, Netherlands, March 1** — A U.N.-backed tribunal opened its doors on Sunday to try suspects in the 2005 assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, a killing that transformed Lebanon’s politics, forced Syria’s military withdrawal and deepened divisions between rival Lebanese camps.

The Special Tribunal for Lebanon, based in a heavily secured former Dutch intelligence building outside The Hague, is the first international court established to prosecute a political assassination as a terrorist crime. It will investigate the truck bombing that killed Hariri and 22 others on Feb. 14, 2005, as his motorcade passed along Beirut’s seafront.

Hariri, a billionaire businessman and dominant postwar political figure, was killed by a massive explosion that ripped through the Saint George Hotel district, leaving a crater in the road and setting nearby buildings and vehicles ablaze. The attack wounded more than 200 people and triggered international outrage.

The tribunal begins work with no defendants in its custody and no public indictments. Its prosecutor, Canadian jurist Daniel Bellemare, takes over from a U.N. investigative commission that spent years probing the bombing. A pre-trial judge, Daniel Fransen of Belgium, will review evidence and any future indictments.

The court’s first president is Antonio Cassese, an Italian jurist and former head of the tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. Lebanese judge Ralph Riachy serves as vice president. The tribunal’s bench includes both international and Lebanese judges, reflecting a hybrid structure meant to combine Lebanese law with international procedure.

Four Lebanese security officials — Jamil al-Sayyed, Ali al-Hajj, Raymond Azar and Mustafa Hamdan — were detained in Lebanon in 2005 in connection with the case, but have not been charged by the new tribunal. Their continued detention has been one of the most politically sensitive issues facing the court as it opens.

The tribunal is funded 49 percent by Lebanon and 51 percent by voluntary contributions from foreign governments. Supporters say the arrangement underscores international backing for accountability. Critics in Lebanon say the court risks becoming a political instrument in a country still divided over Syria’s influence and the role of Hezbollah.

Hariri’s assassination sparked mass demonstrations known as the Cedar Revolution, culminating in the withdrawal of Syrian troops from Lebanon after nearly three decades. Damascus denied involvement in the killing, but the attack intensified pressure on Syria and reshaped Lebanon’s political landscape.

The tribunal’s launch comes as Lebanon remains split between a Western- and Saudi-backed coalition led by Hariri’s son, Saad al-Hariri, and an opposition alliance including Hezbollah and groups close to Syria. Many in the March 14 bloc view the court as a path to justice and sovereignty. Hezbollah and its allies have warned against politicizing the investigation.

Officials at the court said proceedings will follow international fair-trial standards and that trials may be held in absentia, a feature allowed under Lebanese law and incorporated into the tribunal’s statute.

For families of the victims, the opening marks the first formal step toward a judicial accounting four years after the blast. For Lebanon’s rival factions, it also opens a new and potentially volatile chapter in the unresolved struggle over power, foreign influence and the legacy of Hariri’s killing.

**BEIRUT, Lebanon —** The long and politically explosive investigation into the assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri has formally moved onto an international stage, as a U.N.-backed tribunal in The Hague takes up a case that reshaped Lebanon’s politics, ended decades of overt Syrian military presence and deepened the country’s bitter divisions.

The Special Tribunal for Lebanon, established by agreement between the United Nations and Lebanon, is tasked with prosecuting those responsible for the Feb. 14, 2005, bombing that killed Hariri and 21 others on Beirut’s seafront. The attack, carried out by a massive truck bomb as Hariri’s convoy passed near the St. George Hotel, stunned the country and reverberated across the Middle East.

For many Lebanese, the tribunal represents a rare attempt to impose legal accountability in a country where political assassinations have often gone unpunished. For others, particularly critics aligned with Syria and Hezbollah, it has long been viewed with suspicion as a politicized instrument of Western pressure.

Hariri, a billionaire businessman and dominant postwar political figure, served multiple terms as prime minister and was credited by supporters with rebuilding central Beirut after Lebanon’s 1975-1990 civil war. But he also became a central figure in Lebanon’s struggle over sovereignty, particularly as tensions grew between Lebanese political factions and Syria, which for years maintained decisive influence over Beirut’s security and political institutions.

### A killing that transformed Lebanon

The assassination triggered immediate outrage. Hundreds of thousands of Lebanese poured into the streets, demanding the truth about Hariri’s killing and calling for the withdrawal of Syrian troops. The protests became known as the Cedar Revolution and gave rise to the March 14 movement, named after the date in 2005 when a vast anti-Syrian rally filled downtown Beirut.

The March 14 coalition brought together Hariri’s Future Movement, Christian parties including the Lebanese Forces and Kataeb, and Druze leader Walid Jumblatt’s Progressive Socialist Party, among others. Its core demand was an end to Syrian tutelage over Lebanon and the establishment of full Lebanese sovereignty.

Their opponents coalesced around the March 8 alliance, named after a pro-Syrian demonstration held days earlier in 2005. That camp included Hezbollah, the Amal Movement and other parties that credited Syria with supporting resistance against Israel and maintaining Lebanon’s stability after the civil war.

The competing March 14 and March 8 blocs came to define Lebanese politics for years, turning the Hariri case into more than a criminal inquiry. It became a battle over Lebanon’s identity, foreign alliances and the balance of power between state institutions and armed nonstate groups.

### Syria’s long shadow

Syria’s influence in Lebanon dates back to the civil war, when Syrian troops entered the country in 1976 under the banner of an Arab League peacekeeping mission. Over time, Damascus became the dominant power broker in Lebanese affairs, controlling or heavily influencing presidential elections, governments, security agencies and major policy decisions.

The 1989 Taif Agreement, which helped end Lebanon’s civil war, called for the redeployment and eventual withdrawal of Syrian forces. But in practice, Syria’s military and intelligence presence remained entrenched throughout the 1990s and early 2000s. Lebanese politicians who opposed Syrian dominance were marginalized, threatened, exiled or, in some cases, assassinated.

Hariri’s relationship with Damascus was complicated. He governed for years within the Syrian-dominated system, but by 2004 tensions had sharpened, particularly after Syria pushed for the extension of President Émile Lahoud’s term, a move opposed by many Lebanese politicians and criticized internationally. U.N. Security Council Resolution 1559, adopted in September 2004, called for the withdrawal of foreign forces from Lebanon and the disbanding of militias.

After Hariri’s killing, widespread Lebanese protests and intense international pressure forced Syria to withdraw its troops in April 2005, ending nearly three decades of military presence. Damascus denied involvement in the assassination, but the killing left a deep stain on its role in Lebanon and intensified scrutiny of its Lebanese allies.

### From Beirut to The Hague

The move to a tribunal outside Lebanon reflects the sensitivity and danger surrounding the case. Lebanese investigators initially handled the inquiry, aided by a U.N. commission. Early international investigations pointed to a complex plot and raised questions about senior Syrian and Lebanese security officials, though Syria repeatedly denied any role.

The tribunal was created to prosecute those responsible for the Hariri assassination and connected attacks deemed related by the court. Unlike most international courts, it applies Lebanese criminal law while operating under international auspices. It is also notable for allowing trials in absentia, meaning suspects can be tried even if they are not in custody.

Supporters of the court say that feature is necessary given Lebanon’s fractured security environment and the difficulty of arresting politically protected suspects. Critics say it risks producing judgments that will be seen as one-sided or unenforceable.

The tribunal’s establishment followed fierce political disputes in Lebanon. The country’s institutions were repeatedly paralyzed by arguments over cooperation with the court, funding and the broader question of whether international justice could operate in a deeply polarized society. At times, those tensions spilled into the streets, contributing to Lebanon’s recurring instability.

### A country still divided

The Hariri assassination was followed by a wave of other attacks targeting journalists, politicians and security officials associated with anti-Syrian positions. The killings reinforced fears among March 14 supporters that Lebanon was being punished for challenging Syrian authority.

At the same time, Hezbollah and its allies warned that the tribunal could be used to weaken the “resistance” and shift Lebanon into the orbit of the United States, France and Saudi Arabia. Hezbollah, which maintains a powerful armed wing and political presence, has consistently rejected accusations against it and denounced the tribunal as biased.

For Hariri’s supporters, however, the case remains personal and national. His son, Saad Hariri, emerged as a leading figure after the assassination and eventually became prime minister himself. The Future Movement built much of its post-2005 identity around the demand for justice, portraying the tribunal as a test of whether Lebanon could escape the cycle of political violence.

In Beirut, memories of the bombing remain vivid. The site of the attack, near the Mediterranean waterfront, became a place of mourning and political symbolism. Hariri’s grave in downtown Beirut, near the Mohammad Al-Amin Mosque, has long served as a gathering point for supporters.

### Justice and its limits

The tribunal’s move to The Hague offers a measure of distance from Lebanon’s volatile political arena, but it cannot escape the realities that shaped the case. The assassination sits at the intersection of regional rivalries involving Syria, Iran, Saudi Arabia, France and the United States. It also reflects Lebanon’s internal struggle over sovereignty, sectarian power-sharing and the role of armed groups outside state control.

Legal proceedings may establish individual criminal responsibility, but they are unlikely by themselves to resolve the political questions Hariri’s death exposed. Nearly two decades after Syrian troops withdrew, Lebanon remains heavily influenced by regional powers, its state institutions weakened by economic collapse and political paralysis.

Still, for families of the victims and many Lebanese who joined the March 14 demonstrations, the tribunal’s work carries profound symbolic weight. They see it as a challenge to the culture of impunity that has marked Lebanon’s modern history.

As the case proceeds in The Hague, Beirut watches with a mixture of hope, skepticism and fatigue. The assassination of Rafik Hariri changed Lebanon once already. Whether the tribunal can deliver justice accepted across the country remains an open question.
